questions.question: Q: For a distribution with mean = 45, median = 40, and SD = 10, calculate Pearson's skewness coefficient and interpret it.

points.text: Skewness = 3 × (45 – 40) ÷ 10 = 1.5. This is a positive value indicating positive (right) skew.

questions.question: Q: A dataset has Q1 = 20, Q3 = 44. A value of 82 is recorded. Is it an outlier using the 1.5 × IQR rule?

points.text: IQR = 44 – 20 = 24. Upper boundary = 44 + 1.5 × 24 = 80. Since 82 > 80, yes it is an outlier.

questions.question: Q: The data 5, 6, 7, 8, 100 has mean 25.2 and median 7. Why is the median more appropriate?

points.text: The outlier 100 inflates the mean to 25.2, far from most values. The median of 7 is resistant to the outlier and better represents the centre.

questions.question: Q: On a box plot, the right whisker is much longer than the left and the median is near Q1. What does this indicate?

points.text: This indicates positive skew — the data is stretched towards higher values, with a long tail to the right.

questions.question: Q: A value of 12 is recorded in a dataset with mean 50 and SD 18. Is it a potential outlier using the 2 SD rule?

points.text: Distance from mean = |12 – 50| = 38. Since 38 > 2 × 18 = 36, the value 12 is more than 2 SDs from the mean and is a potential outlier.

questions.question: Full-Mark Response A dataset of 10 test scores has Q1 = 35, Q2 = 52, Q3 = 65, mean = 54, and SD = 18. The maximum value is 110. Determine whether the maximum is an outlier and calculate Pearson's skewness coefficient. <div class="

points.text: Outlier test using 1.5 × IQR: IQR = 65 – 35 = 30 Upper boundary = 65 + 1.5 × 30 = 65 + 45 = 110 Since 110 equals (not exceeds) the boundary, it is not classified as an outlier by the 1.5 × IQR rule. It is at the very edge. Pearson's skewness coefficient: Skewness = 3 × (mean – median) ÷ SD = 3 × (54 – 52) ÷ 18 = 6 ÷ 18 = 0.333 Since 0.333 is between –0.5 and 0.5, the distribution is approximately symmetric with a very slight positive skew.
